paper_metadata.title: Higher-Order Portfolio Optimization with Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm

summary: The paper benchmarks QAOA on 100 higher‑order portfolio optimization instances derived from DJIA data, encoded as HUBO Hamiltonians requiring 6–15 qubits. QAOA increases the probability of measuring the optimal state by an average factor of 14.43 over random sampling, but classical baselines outperform QAOA on most metrics (e.g., only 3/100 cases achieve both high objective and good budget utilization vs 50/100 for classical methods). The work mainly demonstrates that HUBO formulations can encode higher‑quality portfolios, not that QAOA currently solves them effectively.

experiments.description: QAOA benchmark on 100 higher-order portfolio optimization instances with skewness/kurtosis terms, compared against classical continuous-variable baselines and exact eigensolvers for small qubit counts.

algorithm.variant: standard QAOA for higher-order unconstrained binary optimization (HUBO) portfolio optimization
algorithm.ansatz: standard QAOA with Hadamard initial layer, problem unitary from higher-order Ising Hamiltonian, and standard X-mixer
algorithm.convergence_criteria: limited number of iterations; optimizer run until completion of the configured iteration budget
algorithm.parameter_initialization: initial parameter values used for the QAOA circuit; exact initialization scheme not specified

problem_formulation.encoding_details: integer portfolio quantities z_i encoded into binary variables with logarithmic overhead; for each asset i, z_i ranges from 0 to floor(C/p_i^tau) and is represented by O(log N) qubits
problem_formulation.objective_function: min_z q2 K(z) - q1 S(z) + q0 z^T c z - mu^T z + lambda (z^T p^tau - C)^2
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: budget constraint encoded as quadratic penalty term; also discusses alternative binary budget encoding to penalize overspending, but main experiments use symmetric penalty (z^T p^tau - C)^2
problem_formulation.problem_hamiltonian: H = sum_{S subset I} alpha_S prod_{i in S} Z_i, with terms up to 4-body interactions from cokurtosis

problem_instance.description: Randomly sampled DJIA portfolio optimization instances with higher-order moments, using 2-10 companies and budgets up to 6000; 100 total instances, with 10 random problems for each qubit count from 6 to 15
problem_instance.dataset_name: Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJIA) stock data

dataset_specification.preprocessing: geometric mean for expected returns; annualization with frequency 252; covariance from arithmetic mean with frequency 252; coskewness and cokurtosis tensors computed from returns

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: downloaded from yfinance; returns computed from closing prices; geometric mean used for mean returns; covariance annualized with f=252; higher moments computed from normalized centered returns; instances filtered to fit within 15 qubits
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: 100 random portfolio optimization problems; QAOA compared against exact eigensolver for <=13 qubits and sparse eigensolver for 14-15 qubits, plus classical continuous-variable baselines; performance summarized across qubit counts and lambda values

implementation_details.classical_solver: SciPy SLSQP for continuous baseline; CVXPY for integer-programming discretization; exact eigensolver for <14 qubits; sparse eigenvalue solver for 14-15 qubits
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: continuous-variable baseline solved with SLSQP then discretized via integer programming
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: min-max normalization of objective values; budget utilization computed; discrete allocations compared

convergence_data.loss_curve_shape: optimizer comparison shown; CMA-ES often achieved lowest average objective

speedup_claims.caveats: The paper does not claim an asymptotic or empirical quantum speedup; it reports comparative solution quality and circuit metrics only.

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: unknown; experiments limited to 6–15 qubits with noiseless simulation and shallow QAOA circuits
limiting_factors: QAOA optimization difficulty on rugged HUBO landscapes
classical continuous optimization baselines outperform QAOA on most metrics
no asymptotic speedup analysis or complexity advantage shown

notes: hardware.type inferred as simulator_other because the paper reports exact eigensolver/sparse eigensolver and circuit metrics, but no real QPU or noisy backend is named for the experiments
num_qubits inferred from the paper's stated inclusion criterion of 6 to 15 qubits and the example encodings; exact per-instance qubit counts vary by problem
circuit_depth not explicitly reported as a numeric value; only gate count/depth comparisons are discussed qualitatively in Fig. 5a
speedup_order set to none_proven because the paper does not claim an asymptotic quantum speedup
Table II shows classical baselines outperform QAOA (e.g., intersection metric: 50 and 46 vs 3 for QAOA).
Authors explicitly state that QAOA solves only a small subset of problems with comparable quality and that improvements are needed.

experiments.description: Resource and allocation comparison between QUBO (mean-variance) and HUBO (higher-order) portfolio formulations, including circuit depth/gate counts, spectral differences, and portfolio allocation divergence.

algorithm.variant: QAOA circuit construction comparison for QUBO vs HUBO portfolio formulations
algorithm.ansatz: standard QAOA with cost Hamiltonians derived from QUBO (|S|<=2) and HUBO (|S|<=4)
algorithm.optimizer: not_applicable (analysis performed using exact spectral calculations)

key_results: Circuit depth and gate counts are larger for HUBO than QUBO formulations (Fig. 5a).
Spectral differences between QUBO and HUBO Hamiltonians are very small for small qubit counts (variance about 1e-9–1e-11) but grow with problem size.
KL divergence analysis shows HUBO allocations remain closer to uniform portfolios, implying greater diversification compared to QUBO solutions.
